newsitem.title: HUNGARY: BUDAPEST BOURSE BULL RUN COULD HIT OBSTACLES.
newsitem.headline: BUDAPEST BOURSE BULL RUN COULD HIT OBSTACLES.

text.p: Hungarian stocks, asserting independence from overseas markets, extended their gains on Wednesday to reach a new record high despite the overnight dip on Wall Street.
"While the Hungarian market is generally dependent on foreign markets, as an emerging market it still has some independence," said Balazs Bathory of Creditansalt Securities.

On Wednesday the BUX index ended at 3,716.42 points, up 24.36 points on the day, hitting the fourth successive high. It was 130 percent up on the start of the year, making Budapest one of the fastest growing exchanges in the world.
Unlike some regional bourses, characterised by local factors and low volume, Budapest usually follows the trend of Wall Street and major European bourses but occasionally goes its own way, as today.

"When Wall Street is going up, Americans put money into mutual funds and when the mutual funds have more money, they put it into other markets, including Budapest," said Frances Cloud, analyst at Nomura Equity Research in London.
For the time being the market is benefiting from good corporate results, a new batch of which are expected late this month, and Hungary's favourable image among foreign investors.
However, analysts see obstacles to Budapest extending a run which has seen it more than double this year.
Cloud said she saw Budapest as fully valued and she expected a downward correction later this year.
Bathory also said the steady rise of the index will run out of steam in the near term.
"The index is advancing but after a few more days of rises we can expect a minor correction on the market," Bathory said. "From a technical point of view it's time for that," he said.
Problems could also be on the horizon if the political row over the Hungarian privatisation process spills over into the stock market and erodes western investor confidence.

The state privatisation agency APV's directors as well as the minister responsible for privatisation were dismissed earlier this month in a scandal over irregular payments of millions of dollars to an adviser.

"It may be that problems being seen on the domestic scene, particularly the problems within the government coalition because of the APV scandal might have the effect of persuading people to take some money out of Hungary," Cloud said. "But at the moment there is no sign of it."
Nathan West, salesman at Daiwa Europe Ltd's central European desk in London, said the privatisation spat was the kind of row investors had to take in their stride.
"These things do tend to blow up occasionally in East European countries and people are a little bit acclimatised to it," said West. "They are not necessarily scared off."
He too sees more steam in the Budapest bull run.
"The Hungarian market still looks reasonably good value... We've got the target for the year-end for Hungary of putting in excess of 3,900 (points)," said West.
On Wednesday December BUX index futures closed at 3,804.00 points, up 29.00.
"There's still a bit of euphoria that these markets have still got some way to go," West said.
"It seems that the fundamentals of the market and international sentiment are actually outweighing any sort of domestic political worries," he added. 161604 GMT oct 96
